routes.description: Establish the resurrection as the best historical explanation by defending the relevant facts, an ordinary probabilistic standard, and a theistic context in which divine action is possible.
routes.successCriteria: The route is complete if the historical data are sufficiently established and the resurrection explains them better than naturalistic alternatives after evidential likelihoods and prior context are considered.

motionBridge.description: Show that God's raising Jesus from the dead is the most probable overall explanation of the established historical facts.

centralBridges.description: Establish the crucifixion, burial, empty tomb, postmortem experiences, and transformed disciples as historical data requiring explanation.
Show that historical proof may rest on comparative probability and that ordinary evidence can establish an extraordinary event through favorable likelihood ratios.
Show that conspiracy, hallucination, and legendary development lack the explanatory power, scope, or historical fit needed to displace resurrection.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply independent theistic context under which a creator's miraculous action is not intrinsically implausible.
Ground the appearance traditions in early and independent sources rather than only in the dates of the completed Gospels.

routes.description: Prevent the resurrection conclusion by challenging the applicable evidential threshold, its prior probability, the reliability of the underlying reports, and the exclusion of natural alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route is complete if evidential caution leaves the resurrection less warranted than skeptical alternatives or leaves the historical premises too uncertain to support a best-explanation conclusion.

motionBridge.description: Show that the historical record does not warrant identifying a divine resurrection as the best explanation of the relevant facts.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish historical facts from the further explanatory inference and require evidence commensurate with the claim's extraordinary character and significance.
Show that a divine raising of the dead carries a sufficiently unfavorable prior probability that weak naturalistic accounts can remain preferable.
Challenge whether group appearances and related reports are reliably established rather than products of sparse attestation or legendary development.
Provide a natural account under which sincere disciples could mistakenly believe Jesus had risen without deliberate fabrication.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why an omnipotent agent intent on widespread resurrection belief would be expected to provide clearer or more abundant evidence.
Use differences across the Gospel sequence to test whether increasingly elaborate appearance narratives reflect historical development.

sections.title: Historical proof and evidential threshold
sections.rationale: The motion depends on what historical proof requires and whether the extraordinary character and significance of resurrection alter the evidence needed for the explanatory conclusion.

sections.title: Prior probability and divine action
sections.rationale: Comparative explanation requires an account of resurrection's antecedent plausibility, including whether theism changes the prior and whether divine intentions affect expected evidence.

sections.title: Historical data and source reliability
sections.rationale: The explanatory comparison can proceed only if the empty tomb, appearances, and related facts are sufficiently grounded in early and independent historical testimony.

sections.title: Naturalistic alternatives and explanatory scope
sections.rationale: The best-explanation burden turns on whether sincere mistake, hallucination, conspiracy, or related alternatives explain the disciples' beliefs and the empty tomb without resurrection.

chunk-001:c004.proposition: Historical inquiry can establish facts surrounding the alleged resurrection but cannot directly prove the resurrection itself, which remains an inference to the best explanation.

chunk-001:c005.proposition: Showing that the resurrection is the most probable historical explanation constitutes proof in the ordinary historical sense, though not mathematical demonstration.

chunk-001:c006.proposition: The resurrection's extraordinary nature, moral importance, and asserted divine purpose justify demanding substantially stronger evidence than ordinary historical claims require.

chunk-001:c007.proposition: The resurrection should face the same epistemic historical standard as other events, while Christianity's potential benefits may additionally provide pragmatic justification for belief.

chunk-001:c008.proposition: A God who strongly wants humanity to believe in the resurrection should provide more evidence than the roughly ordinary historical record that appears available.

chunk-001:c009.proposition: An extraordinary event can be established by ordinary evidence when that evidence is much more probable if the event occurred than if it did not.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-01.proposition: Even weak naturalistic alternatives may remain more credible than resurrection because divine raising of the dead has an exceptionally unfavorable prior probability for an atheist.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-02.proposition: Miracles are not intrinsically implausible if God exists, so resurrection evidence should be assessed within the theistic context supplied by independent arguments for a creator.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-03.proposition: Five widely accepted historical facts—crucifixion, burial, empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and transformed disciples—are best explained by the resurrection under standard explanatory criteria.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-04.proposition: A conspiracy explanation is implausible because the earliest disciples sincerely endured suffering for their proclamation and would not have invented an individual resurrection alien to first-century Jewish expectations.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-05.proposition: The disciples could have sincerely died for a mistaken belief, with grief-induced hallucination providing a natural explanation for their conviction that Jesus had risen.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-06.proposition: Hallucination lacks explanatory power because Jewish expectations would produce visions of Jesus in heaven rather than belief in an isolated resurrection, and it does not explain the empty tomb.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-07.proposition: The underlying reports may be unreliable because group appearances have sparse and uneven attestation and the earliest Gospel narrates no post-resurrection appearance.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-08.proposition: The core resurrection data are broadly accepted, while postmortem experiences are supported by very early Pauline tradition, multiple independent Gospel attestations, and Mark's foreshadowing of appearances.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-09.proposition: The Gospel sequence suggests legendary development because Mark offers only a prediction, Matthew supplies a doubted Galilean appearance, and later Gospels add increasingly numerous and fanciful episodes.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-10.proposition: Dating the completed Gospels does not date their underlying traditions; independent early sources behind the Gospels and Paul make late legendary development unreasonable.
